title: How Does Netflix Play a Movie Without Downloading It?
sources: Mux, 'What is adaptive bitrate streaming (ABR)?' (mux.com/articles/abr-adaptive-bitrate): video is 'encoded into multiple versions at different bitrates and resolutions (renditions)'; each version is 'divided into small video segments', 'typically 2-10 seconds'; 'As chunks download faster than they play, the buffer fills up'; if the connection 'threatens to buffer, ABR adjusts the video's bitrate load to reduce buffering', prioritising 'continuous playback over visual fidelity'
Wikipedia 'Adaptive bitrate streaming': source encoded at multiple bit rates, each split into small multi-second parts; the client switches between streams depending on available bandwidth

Netflix, 'How Netflix works with ISPs around the globe to deliver a great viewing experience' (about.netflix.com, 2016): connections to Open Connect are 'always free'; Netflix gives qualifying ISPs Open Connect Appliances; once installed in an ISP's data center 'almost all Netflix content is served from the local OCAs'; most members get their video 'from a server that's either inside of, or directly connected to, their ISP's network within their local region'
Netflix Open Connect (openconnect.netflix.com) and Wikipedia 'Open Connect': Netflix's own CDN; appliances provided to ISPs at no charge and filled with content during off-peak hours

lines.text: How does Netflix play a movie
Well, the movie is chopped into tiny chunks,
and the app grabs them one by one,
lines.caps: AND THE APP *GRABS | THEM ONE BY *ONE

lines.text: a little ahead of where you're watching.
That saved up stretch is called the buffer.
Every chunk is stored in lots of qualities,
so when your Wi-Fi slows down,
the app quietly switches to a blurrier version
Those chunks often don't travel far at all.
Netflix gives free servers to internet providers,
so your movie is already waiting close to home.
lines.caps: SO YOUR *MOVIE | IS ALREADY *WAITING | *CLOSE TO HOME

lines.text: You're never watching the whole movie,
